help.part.reports.title: Reports
help.part.reports.blurb: What the family DOES, read back — the work, the elections, the meetings and the offices.
help.gatherings-report.title: Gatherings Report
help.gatherings-report.summary: Every gathering with how much of its work is done, what is overdue, and what its tasks claim against the budget.
help.gatherings-report.what-it-is.b0: [Gatherings](/reporting/gatherings) under **Reporting** is one row per gathering: how many of its tasks are approved, how many are late, how many nobody is holding, and — where you can see the money — what its task lines add up to against what it budgeted.
help.gatherings-report.what-it-is.b1: It changes nothing and creates nothing. Every row links into [Gatherings](/gatherings), where the thing itself lives.
help.gatherings-report.what-it-is.b2: **Cancelled gatherings are left out entirely**, rows and totals alike. Their open tasks are not work anybody owes, and counting them would leave a family that cancelled one thing permanently in the red on every figure here.
help.gatherings-report.overdue.heading: What counts as overdue
help.gatherings-report.overdue.b0: A task is overdue when **its date has passed and nobody has approved it**. That includes one that has been submitted and not yet ruled on — the work may well be done, but it is still outstanding from the organizer’s side, and this is the organizer’s report. A task sent back counts too.
help.gatherings-report.overdue.b1: **A task with no due date is never overdue.** Nothing was promised for a particular day, so there is no day it can be late relative to.
help.gatherings-report.money.heading: The money columns
help.gatherings-report.money.b0: **Allocated** is what the gathering’s task lines claim, shown against what the gathering set aside. It is marked when the lines claim more than the budget — which is a plan to fix rather than an error, so it is not shown in red.
help.gatherings-report.money.b1: The two money figures appear only if your family is on a plan that includes the gathering budget band and you have been granted it. Without either, the columns are simply not there — a column of dashes would be a claim that the family budgeted nothing.
help.elections-report.title: Elections Report
help.elections-report.summary: Turnout per election, how many stood, and which offices nobody put a name forward for.
help.elections-report.what-it-is.heading: What it answers
help.elections-report.what-it-is.b0: [Elections](/reporting/elections) under **Reporting** is one row per published election: which area it covers, what phase it is in, how many nominations it drew and how many were accepted, and what the turnout was.
help.elections-report.what-it-is.b1: **Drafts are not counted.** A draft has no dates, no ballot and no electorate, so a 0% turnout row for one would be a report about an election nobody has been told about.
help.elections-report.turnout.heading: How turnout is worked out
help.elections-report.turnout.b0: **Turnout counts people, not ballots.** Somebody voting for three offices in one election is one voter. The bottom half of the figure is who could have voted: every approved member for a national election, the members of one chapter for a chapter election, and the members of every chapter in a region for a regional one — the same rule that decides who sees the election in the first place.
help.elections-report.turnout.b1: An election whose area holds no approved members reads **n/a** rather than 0%. Nobody could have voted in it, and 0% would read as an election everybody ignored.
help.elections-report.unopposed.heading: Offices nobody stood for
help.elections-report.unopposed.b0: An office with no **accepted** nomination has nothing on the ballot. A nomination the nominee has not accepted does not count — it puts no name in front of anybody.
help.elections-report.unopposed.b1: This is the figure worth acting on before the nomination window closes, which is why it is one of the four at the top of the page.
help.meetings-report.title: Meetings Report
help.meetings-report.summary: How often the family meets, how big each room was, and who answers when a vote is called.
help.meetings-report.what-it-is.heading: What it answers
help.meetings-report.what-it-is.b0: [Meetings](/reporting/meetings) under **Reporting** has two tables. The first is one row per meeting — its date, who took the minutes, how many were in the room, how many topics it took up and how many votes were cast. The second is one row per relative: how many meetings they were asked to, how many they voted in, and how many they minuted.
help.meetings-report.what-it-is.b1: Every meeting row links into [Meeting Minutes](/library/meeting-minutes), which is where the record itself lives.
help.meetings-report.not-attendance.head: Why nothing here says “attendance”
help.meetings-report.not-attendance.b0: **Nothing in GENORRA records who actually turned up.** There is no check-in. So this reports the two things it can count and neither of them is attendance:
help.meetings-report.not-attendance.b1.i: The attendee list — who was invited when the meeting was scheduled.

How many of those meetings the person answered a vote in. It is the only positive evidence anybody was in the room, and it is a floor rather than a count: a quiet meeting with no vote called produces none of it.
help.meetings-report.not-attendance.b2: Averaging the two into an attendance rate would be a figure no row in the database supports — and it is exactly the sort of number that gets quoted in a meeting a year later.
help.meetings-report.minuted.heading: Minuted against held
help.meetings-report.minuted.b0: **Minuted** counts the meetings somebody has closed. Closing is what turns a meeting into a record — no more topics, no more notes, no more votes — so the gap between the two figures is the family’s backlog of meetings nobody has signed off.
help.board-report.title: Board & Offices Report
help.board-report.summary: Every office the family has defined, who holds it, and which ones are standing empty.
help.board-report.what-it-is.heading: What it answers
help.board-report.what-it-is.b0: [Board & Offices](/reporting/board) under **Reporting** lists every board position the family has defined, in the family’s own order, with whoever holds it — and, where nobody does, the word **Vacant**.
help.board-report.what-it-is.b1: It changes nothing. Defining a position and handing it out is **Members → Organization**, which is a separate permission.
help.board-report.what-it-is.b2: That separation is the point of this screen existing at all: a nominations committee can be shown where the gaps are without being given the power to change the roster.
help.board-report.vacancies.heading: Vacancies are the finding
help.board-report.vacancies.b0: **Every position is a row, including the empty ones**, and **Vacant** is one of the four figures at the top. A report that listed only filled offices could not state its most useful fact.
help.board-report.vacancies.b1: The rows stay in the family’s own order rather than putting the vacancies first, so this can be read side by side with the list on **Members → Organization**. The colour is what makes a gap findable.
help.board-report.two-hats.heading: Holding more than one office
help.board-report.two-hats.b0: A section appears when somebody holds two or more. That is not a problem in itself — a small chapter often has one person doing two jobs — but it is usually the sign of a gap somebody has quietly covered, which is worth knowing before the next election.
help.board-report.two-hats.b1: An office held for a particular region or chapter says which beside the name. The same title at two levels is two different offices: a National President and a Chapter President are separate rows.
